breeds.name: Norwegian Elkhound (Grey)
breeds.estimate_note: Primary FCI-St N°242 (1999) has NO historical section -- confirmed by reading the full standard text (2026-08-09), it is pure conformation/appearance description. The "~5000-4000 BCE, Viste Cave dog skeletons identified as Elkhound-type by Professor Brinchmann of Bergen Museum" claim traces only to dog-breed enthusiast sites (Showsight Magazine, National Purebred Dog Day, Sons of Norway, NEAA), all repeating the same unattributed identification with no accessible original publication, journal, or DOI -- unlike Akita's equivalent claim (see mrca_lineage_id: kamikuroiwa-jomon-dog), this could not be traced to a real citable source despite a genuine search attempt (2026-08-09): the Wikipedia "Alex Brinchmann" is a pediatrician/novelist, not the zoologist being referenced; the one real academic reference found for the Viste site, M. Degerbol's 1951 Stavanger Museum faunal study, could not be confirmed as the actual source of the Elkhound identification. Treat as unverified breed lore, not a citable archaeological/genetic finding -- see PROCESS.md Open threads for the follow-up (needs Norwegian-language archive access).
breeds.notes: Downgraded from anchor to vague 2026-08-09 after a citation-verification pass (same check that resolved Akita/Middle Asian Ovtcharka) found no real source behind the Viste Cave claim -- see origin_estimate_note. origin_estimate_value left as-is (not cleared/migrated to mrca_lineage_id) since there's no verifiable source to cite in ancestor_lineages.csv; this is a genuine tier-1/tier-2 conflation the same way Akita's was, just blocked on sourcing rather than resolved. Not logged to needs_verification.csv -- that queue is for lower-reasoning-model deferrals per PROCESS.md; this verification was already attempted directly by a higher-reasoning session and reached a dead end, which is a different (and more final, pending better source access) state than 'not yet checked.'

breeds.name: Ibizan Hound (Podenco Ibicenco)
breeds.estimate_note: French-language FCI-St N°89 (04.02.2000): "il s'agit donc d'un type de chien primitif et rustique... dont on peut voir la représentation dans les tombes de pharaons et sur des pièces de musées, ce qui en fait remonter l'origine à 3400 ans A.C." (traced to 3400 years BC via depictions in pharaohs' tombs and museum pieces).
breeds.notes: CAVEAT — the same 2004 Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center DNA study that debunked the Pharaoh Hound's Egyptian-origin myth (see pharaoh-hound row) explicitly named the Ibizan Hound too: found NOT to be an ancient breed, but a modern re-creation, likely developed by breeders and only resembling ancient tomb art coincidentally/by selective breeding toward that look. More likely real origin per the same research: Phoenician traders brought similar hunting dogs to the Balearics ~800-600 BCE, much later than 3400 BCE and probably not a continuous line to the modern breed. The FCI standard's own historical claim is the kind of traditional myth genetics has since contradicted — DON'T take the 3400 BCE figure at face value; treat it as "what the official standard says," clearly flagged as scientifically disputed, not as the project's best date estimate.

breeds.name: Saluki
breeds.estimate_note: SECONDARY SOURCE (AKC page itself has nothing but "ancient"): a golden dog pendant at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, excavated at the Sumerian city of Uruk, depicts a curly-tailed, tall-eared dog consistent with Saluki type, dated ~3300 BCE (early Bronze Age Mesopotamia).
breeds.notes: This is one archaeological artifact showing a Saluki-*type* dog existed, not proof of an unbroken breed lineage to today's AKC Saluki — treat as "earliest depiction of the type," same epistemic category as the Ibizan/Pharaoh Hound tomb-art claims below, which turned out to be misleading. Worth noting as a caveat rather than treating as settled. Linked to village_dog_population_id: middle-eastern-village-dog-clade 2026-08-09 (Brown et al. 2011 Y-chromosome study -- desert-bred Salukis cluster entirely within the Middle Eastern village dog clade, ~6,820 BP). Additional deeper-tier fact, not a replacement for this row's own tier-2 date -- same pattern as Chihuahua/precontact-american-dog.

village.name: Middle Eastern village dog clade
village.region: Middle East (Egypt, Lebanon, Qatar, Turkey, Afghanistan sampled)
village.diverged_from: reciprocally monophyletic sister clade to the Southeast Asian village dog Y-chromosome lineage
village.estimate_note: Brown et al. 2011 Y-chromosome (paternal lineage) analysis found Middle Eastern village dogs form a reciprocally monophyletic clade distinct from the Southeast Asian village dog clade, estimated age 6,820 BP (95% CI 3,931-9,709 BP). Desert-bred Salukis clustered entirely within this clade, sharing six haplotypes with regional village dogs.
village.notes: Second real dated village-dog population found (2026-08-09), after the Taiwan/Indonesian pilot -- schema was deliberately not generalized further until a second real case showed up (see village_dog_populations_schema.md). Y-chromosome-only (paternal lineage), wide confidence interval (3,931-9,709 BP) -- weaker/narrower evidence than Zhang et al. 2020's whole-genome dating for the Taiwan/Indonesian clade, hence anchor not rich. Does not establish when the modern standardized Saluki breed itself was founded, only that it clusters within this dated regional clade -- Saluki's own tier-2 date (FCI/AKC's ~3300 BCE Sumerian-pendant claim) is separate, unaffected, and itself flagged in that row's notes as an unverified resemblance-based claim (same epistemic category as the debunked Pharaoh Hound/Ibizan Hound tomb-art dates) -- this clade date doesn't confirm or contradict that specific number, just establishes a deeper, genetically-real clade Saluki belongs to.
village.source_citation: Brown et al. 2011, "Phylogenetic distinctiveness of Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian village dog Y chromosomes illuminates dog origins," PLoS ONE 6(12):e28496

breeds.name: Basenji
breeds.estimate_note: Primary FCI standard (2000) has NO historical section. SECONDARY SOURCE instead: small dogs matching Basenji size/shape are painted at owners' feet in tombs from the Great Pyramid of Khufu complex (IV Dynasty Egypt, ~2700 BCE); rock art in Libya dated ~6000 BCE shows similar pariah-type hunting dogs. Basenji is also a longstanding candidate for the visual inspiration behind Anubis/jackal-headed imagery.
breeds.notes: Unlike Pharaoh/Ibizan Hound (see below), Basenji's ancient-lineage claim has real genomic backing: it consistently comes out as one of the more basal/divergent clades in genome-wide studies (Parker et al. 2017 and earlier vonHoldt et al. 2010 work on African village dogs) — so the archaeological art claim and the genetics point the same direction here, unlike the Mediterranean pharaoh-type hounds.

breeds.name: Middle Asian Ovtcharka
breeds.also_known_as: Central Asian Shepherd Dog (FCI's own name for this breed; also a separate row in this dataset, key=central-asian-shepherd-dog — likely a duplicate, see tasks.md); Alabai; Turkmen Alabai; Sredneasiatskaya Ovcharka
breeds.origin_country: Central Asia (region: Caspian Sea to China, Southern Ural to Afghanistan)
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°335 (2010): "formed as a breed from natural selection during more than four thousand years" (= pre-~2010 BCE). "The work with the breed started in the USSR in the 1930s." SECONDARY GENETIC SOURCE (2026-08-09 targeted verification, cf. Chow Chow/Wang et al. 2017 precedent): no whole-genome study dates this breed specifically the way Wang et al. 2017 dated Chow Chow. However, Zhang et al. 2025, "Genomic evidence for the Holocene codispersal of dogs and humans across Eastern Eurasia," Science — 73 ancient dog genomes across ~10,000 years, Siberia to the Central Asian Steppe — found dogs moved together with Eurasian Steppe pastoralist populations into Western China during the Early Bronze Age (~4,000 years ago), independently corroborating the order of magnitude of FCI's timeframe via ancient DNA rather than archaeology/lore. Separately, Perfilyeva et al. 2024 (Scientific Reports, Kazakh Tobet Dogs) found mtDNA D-loop evidence of shared ancestry between Central Asian Shepherd Dog, Kazakh Tobet, and Turkish Akbash, but gave no divergence-time estimate.
breeds.notes: Genetics search completed 2026-08-09 (targeted verification per PROCESS.md step 6, parallel to the Chow Chow precedent). Unlike Chow Chow, no breed-specific divergence-time study exists. The Zhang et al. 2025 ancient-DNA finding is a genuine independent corroboration of FCI's ~4,000-year order of magnitude (dogs demonstrably moved with Central Asian/Steppe pastoralists at that time) — a materially different outcome than Pharaoh Hound/Ibizan Hound, where genetics specifically contradicted a similar ancient claim. Still not proof of an unbroken lineage to the modern standardized breed (formalized USSR 1930s) — same pattern as Akita/Norwegian Elkhound. Confidence tier stays anchor, not upgraded to rich: one corroborating data point, not multiple independent dated references, and it doesn't sharpen FCI's own number. See data/supplemental/middle-asian-ovtcharka.txt for full research.

breeds.name: Central Asian Shepherd Dog
breeds.also_known_as: Middle Asian Ovtcharka (also a separate row in this dataset, key=middle-asian-ovtcharka — likely a duplicate, see tasks.md); Alabai; Turkmen Alabai; Sredneasiatskaya Ovcharka
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°335: "formed as a breed from natural selection during more than four thousand years in the vast territory from the Caspian Sea to China." UKC: "For thousands of years...used by nomadic tribes of Central Asia." Genomic studies confirm basal breed status.
breeds.notes: FCI primary source states 4000+ year claim; UKC corroborates. Genomic studies support ancient status but specific timeframe unverified.

breeds.name: Dingo
breeds.estimate_note: CKC page Cloudflare-blocked; Wikipedia and peer-reviewed studies used. Wikipedia: "Temporal range: Holocene (3,450 years BP – recent)." Scientific Reports 2018 (Madura Cave): dingoes in southern Australia between 3348 and 3081 years ago (direct radiocarbon dating). Genetic studies suggest origins in Asia (likely China via Southeast Asia); arrival possibly connected to Indian genome influx ~4000 BP.
breeds.notes: The dingo is a feral/semi-wild dog, not a kennel-standardized breed — its presence on this list reflects its cultural significance and unique lineage. Best arrival estimate: ~3,450 BP (~1500 BCE), based on Madura Cave radiocarbon dating (oldest confirmed bones in Australia). Closely related to New Guinea Singing Dog (shared lineage ~3500 BP with Oceanic human migration). Asian origin (likely China via Southeast Asia/Taiwan). Note: some sources say 3000-8000 years ago — the 3450 BP Wikipedia temporal range is the most supported figure. See supplemental file for full citation details.

breeds.name: New Guinea Singing Dog
breeds.estimate_note: CKC page Cloudflare-blocked; Wikipedia and PNAS studies used. Genetic studies: "the New Guinea singing dog lineage diverged from East Asian dog populations around 3,500 years ago, coinciding with human dispersal to Oceania." PNAS 2021: New Guinea Highland wild dogs are genetically basal to both the dingo and the NGSD. First Western documentation: Torres expedition 1606 (dogs described as "small dumb dogs that neither bark nor howl").
breeds.notes: The NGSD is a wild/feral dog isolated in the New Guinea Highlands — not a standardized kennel breed. Its captive population is descended from a small number captured in the 1950s-70s. The wild population (New Guinea Highland wild dog) was rediscovered via camera traps in 2016 and confirmed genetically as the original NGSD (PNAS 2021). Shares ~3500-year origin timing with the dingo (both arrived with human dispersal into Oceania). First documented 1606 (Torres expedition); formally described 1897 (MacGregor, Mount Scratchley). See supplemental file.

breeds.name: Maltese
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'In a list of dogs existing at the time of Aristotle (384-322 B.C.) is mentioned a breed of little dogs to which is attributed the Latin name canes melitenses... favourite companion of the matrons of Ancient Rome, praised by Strabon, Latin poet of the first century A.D.'
breeds.notes: Direct genetic continuity between ancient canes melitenses and the modern Maltese has not been established. Treat as earliest documented type, not proof of unbroken lineage.

breeds.name: Alaskan Malamute
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia (Thule people): the Thule Tradition lasted from about 200 BCE to 1600 CE. This date describes the broader Thule culture (ancestors of the Malimiut Inupiaq who bred the Alaskan Malamute), not a Malamute-specific founding event -- no dated record exists of when the Malimiut Inupiaq themselves began developing their distinct sled dog. Kept as the best available landrace-tier proxy (origin_estimate_basis: cultural_proxy) rather than cleared to none, since it's at least a real, independently-dated historical/cultural anchor.
breeds.notes: origin_estimate_basis flag added 2026-08-09: this date is about the people (Thule culture), not direct evidence of the dog -- see breed_origins_schema.md's origin_estimate_basis column. Also shares the Zhokhov Island MRCA with Siberian Husky and Greenland Dog (mrca_lineage_id) -- all three trace to the same ~9,500-year-old ancestor; this 200 BCE figure is a separate, more recent tier (landrace formation), not a competing age claim.

mrca.name: Zhokhov Island Siberian sled dog
mrca.estimate_note: Sinding et al. 2020 sequenced a ~9,500-year-old dog genome from Zhokhov Island, northeastern Siberia (associated with early sled-dog technology) alongside 10 modern Greenland sled dogs; found Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute, and Greenland sled dog all share the major part of their genome with this ancient dog. Greenland sled dog shows the least admixture with other dog populations since this split -- the basis of its 'oldest/most original breed' reputation (Guinness World Records, 2020) -- a claim about genetic purity, not an earlier founding date than Husky or Malamute, which trace to the identical ancestor.
mrca.source_citation: Sinding et al. 2020, "Arctic-adapted dogs emerged at the Pleistocene-Holocene transition," Science 368(6498):1495-1499

breeds.name: Chinese Shar-Pei
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'existed for hundreds of years in the provinces bordering the South China Sea.' Secondary: statues resembling Shar-Pei found from Han Dynasty period (c. 200 BC); 13th-century Chinese manuscript describes wrinkled dog with Shar-Pei characteristics; DNA confirms ancient basal breed status.
breeds.notes: FCI standard (1999) gives only 'hundreds of years' with no date. Han Dynasty (~200 BC) statue evidence and 13th-century manuscript from secondary sources (CSPCA). DNA studies confirm basal ancient breed. Nearly extinct by 1970s; revived through American breeding. AKC recognition 1992.

breeds.name: Jindo
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°334: "many authorities agree that this breed has existed for several thousands of years in the Island of Jindo... the Jindo Dog is indigenous to Korea." Genetics (PMC 2017, PLoS ONE 2017): "the breed originated in Korea about 2,000 years ago." The FCI's "several thousands" is the lore; the genetics anchor is ~2000 years ago (~0 CE).
breeds.notes: Natural Monument of Korea No. 53, designated 1962. Genetics confirm ~2000-year-old Korean indigenous breed with "maternally unique phylogenetic history" — not part of major phylogenetic groups. FCI standard (2004) says "several thousands of years" but genetics places it at the ~2000-year end of that range. Isolation on Jindo Island historically maintained breed purity. Shares ancestry with Akita within East Asian basal breeds.

breeds.name: Neapolitan Mastiff
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°197: "descendant of the great Roman Mastiff described by Columelle in the first century A.D. in his book de re rustica...Widespread all over Europe by the Roman legions...re-selected since 1947."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source. Two dated refs: 1st century CE (Columelle) + 1947 re-selection.

breeds.name: Tibetan Mastiff
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°230: "From the mentioning by Aristoteles (384-322 b.C.) to the famous writings of Marco Polo, who went to Asia in 1271...sent to Queen Victoria in 1847...early recorded litter 1898 in the Berlin Zoo."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC study guide is Kaggle primary source. Four dated refs: Aristotle 384 BC, Marco Polo 1271, Queen Victoria 1847, Berlin Zoo 1898.

breeds.name: Irish Wolfhound
breeds.estimate_note: "Irish Wolfhounds were already well established in Ireland in the first century A.D. The first written account of the breed appears in 391 AD."
breeds.notes: Also: first classes given at the Dublin kennel club show in 1879; first breed standard written and breed club formed in 1885. One of the richest historical summaries found so far.

breeds.name: Italian Greyhound
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'the breed arrived in Italy at the outset of the 5th century BC. Its greatest development occurred during the era of the Renaissance at the court of the nobles.'
breeds.notes: FCI also claims Egyptian pharaoh court origin, supported only by art (tomb imagery; vase/bowl representations in Laconie/Greece). Egyptian claim is art-resemblance based — no genetic study specifically confirmed Italian Greyhound as truly ancient. 5th century BC arrival in Italy is from FCI primary source, based on Greek vase art. Renaissance development at Italian noble courts is well-attested historically.

breeds.name: Lhasa Apso
breeds.estimate_note: FCI has no historical date. Secondary: when Tibet converted to Buddhism (~7th century CE), breeders developed type resembling lion; breed known in Tibet by 800 AD. DNA analysis confirms among world's most ancient breeds. FCI: 'first Apsos arrived in Britain in the early 1920s... breed club established in Britain in 1933.'
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no dated historical summary. DNA studies (Parker et al.) confirm Lhasa Apso as ancient/basal breed. Used as temple guard dogs; never sold, only given as gifts in Tibet. UK breed club 1933; AKC recognition 1935.

breeds.name: Bloodhound
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°84: "presumed to descend from black or black and tan hounds hunting in packs which were used in the 7th century by the monk Hubert...In the 11th century these dogs were imported into England by William the Conqueror."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source. Two dated refs: 7th century CE (St. Hubert/monk Hubert) + 11th century (William the Conqueror).

breeds.name: Kuvasz
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°54: "His ancestors came into the Carpathian basin at the time of occupation by the Magyars" (~895 CE). "the Kuvasz was the preferred hunting dog at the time of King Matthias Corvinus" (1458-1490 CE).
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source. Two dated refs: Magyar occupation ~895 CE + King Matthias 1458-1490 CE.

breeds.name: Komondor
breeds.estimate_note: "Old-established Hungarian herding breed of Asiatic origin. His original ancestors almost certainly came with the migrating Old Magyars... to the Carpathian basin." No date given in the FCI standard itself. CONFIRMED against a history source (2026-08-09): the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin is a well-documented historical event -- Arpad led the Magyars across the north-eastern Carpathian passes in autumn 895 CE, with the conquest complete by the end of summer 900 CE (contemporary Byzantine and Old Church Slavonic sources, including the Life of Saint Naum, c. 924). This date describes the Magyar people's migration, not direct evidence of their dogs specifically -- origin_estimate_basis: cultural_proxy.
breeds.notes: Upgraded from a pending 'treat as anchor once confirmed' note to a confirmed anchor 2026-08-09 -- the Magyar conquest date (895-900 CE) is now verified against contemporary historical sources rather than assumed. origin_estimate_basis: cultural_proxy, since this dates the Magyar migration itself, not direct archaeological/genetic evidence of the dog.

breeds.name: Greenland Dog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°274 (2022): "one of the world's oldest breeds and has since ancient times been the Inuits' only sledge dog" — no specific date given. Secondary: 2025 Science study (Qimmeq genomes) found Inuit arrived in Greenland 800-1200 years ago (~800-1200 CE), bringing these dogs. Thule expansion across the American Arctic ~2000 BP (0 CE); deeper Siberian sled dog lineage ~9500 BP.
breeds.notes: The Greenland Dog (Qimmeq) arrived in Greenland with Inuit/Thule peoples ~800-1200 CE. Genetics (2025 Science study) show the breed has remained genetically consistent back to the earliest known sled dogs. Origin date here refers to Greenland-specific establishment, not the broader Thule/Siberian sled dog lineage. origin_estimate_basis: direct, since the ~800-1200 CE arrival date comes from genetic dating of the dogs themselves (Qimmeq genomes), not just human archaeology. ON THE 'OLDEST DOG BREED' CLAIM (2026-08-09): Guinness World Records credits Greenland Dog as the oldest breed, citing Sinding et al. 2020 -- but that study found Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute, AND Greenland Dog all share the identical ~9,500-year-old Zhokhov Island ancestor (see mrca_lineage_id / ancestor_lineages.csv). What actually distinguishes Greenland Dog is that it shows the LEAST admixture with other dog populations since that shared split -- a genetic-purity claim, not an earlier founding date than its two Arctic siblings. All three are equally 'old' by ancestor-lineage; only Greenland Dog is the least-changed descendant of it.

mrca.name: Zhokhov Island Siberian sled dog
mrca.estimate_note: Sinding et al. 2020 sequenced a ~9,500-year-old dog genome from Zhokhov Island, northeastern Siberia (associated with early sled-dog technology) alongside 10 modern Greenland sled dogs; found Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute, and Greenland sled dog all share the major part of their genome with this ancient dog. Greenland sled dog shows the least admixture with other dog populations since this split -- the basis of its 'oldest/most original breed' reputation (Guinness World Records, 2020) -- a claim about genetic purity, not an earlier founding date than Husky or Malamute, which trace to the identical ancestor.
mrca.source_citation: Sinding et al. 2020, "Arctic-adapted dogs emerged at the Pleistocene-Holocene transition," Science 368(6498):1495-1499

breeds.name: Kangal Dog
breeds.estimate_note: UKC: "Beginning in the 11th Century, nomadic Turkic tribes who migrated into modern day Turkey most likely brought along their own working livestock dogs." Named for Kangal District of Sivas Province, Central Turkey.
breeds.notes: UKC breed standard used as primary source.

breeds.name: Pembroke Welsh Corgi
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'the lineage of the Pembroke Welsh Corgi has been traced back to AD 1107' when Flemish weavers, invited by Henry I to settle in Pembrokeshire, brought Spitz-type and Schipperke ancestors.
breeds.notes: Alternate kaggle key for Pembroke Welsh Corgi — same breed as key 'pembroke-welsh-corgi'. Kaggle lists origin as Wales (vs. Great Britain in that entry). FCI has no historical summary section; data from Wikipedia. Modern standardized breed first shown 1925; KC recognition 1928.

breeds.name: Chihuahua
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'at the time of the Toltec civilization, were captured and domesticated by the natives. Representations of a Toy dog called Techichi which lived in Tula were used as decorations on town architecture.' Toltec capital Tula active c.900-1168 CE.
breeds.notes: Pre-Columbian origin genetically confirmed, citation corrected 2026-08-09: the previous "Perri et al. 2021 (Science)" citation could not be verified (no such paper found; Perri is a real co-author, but on Ni Leathlobhair et al. 2018, not a 2021 paper) -- replaced with the real sources. Traced the DOI 10.1038/s41586-020-03082-x (the likely source of the confusion, since Perri is a real co-author on it): it's Perri et al. 2021, "Dire wolves were the last of an ancient New World canid lineage," Nature 591:87-91 -- sequenced 5 dire wolf genomes, found dire wolves split from living canids ~5.7 million years ago with no gene flow to grey wolves/coyotes. Confirmed unrelated to Chihuahua/pre-Columbian dog ancestry -- a different species entirely, not just a wrong year/journal. Don't re-verify this specific DOI again if it resurfaces. Turner then found the likely actual intended paper (2026-08-09): Perri et al. 2021, "Dog domestication and the dual dispersal of people and dogs into the Americas," PNAS 118(6):e2010083118 -- real author/year/topic match, just the wrong journal (PNAS not Science) and no Chihuahua-specific percentage in it (that's still Bergstrom et al. 2020's contribution; Perri 2021 gives the ~15,000-year arrival timing, corroborating Ni Leathlobhair 2018's ~14,600-year figure). Added as a third source on the precontact-american-dog lineage. Ni Leathlobhair et al. 2018 (Science) established the precontact American dog lineage (see mrca_lineage_id: precontact-american-dog); Bergstrom et al. 2020 (Science) found ~4% of that ancestry survives in modern Chihuahuas specifically. This is a minority-ancestry component, not the breed's primary lineage -- the FCI's own Toltec-era Techichi date (900-1168 CE) is independent evidence and stays as this row's tier-2 date, unaffected by this addition.

mrca.name: Pre-contact American dog lineage
mrca.estimate_note: Ni Leathlobhair et al. 2018 sequenced 71 mitochondrial + 7 nuclear genomes from ancient North American and Siberian dogs spanning ~9,000 years. All sampled precontact American dogs (PCDs) formed a monophyletic lineage descended from Siberian dogs introduced via early human migration(s) ~17,500-13,000 years ago, sharing a common ancestor ~14,600 years ago (95% HPD 16,484-12,965 ya) -- diverged from an ancestor shared with the Zhokhov Island dogs (see zhokhov-siberian-sled-dog) ~1,000 years earlier. Critically, this lineage was NOT domesticated locally from North American wolves. Corroborated by Perri et al. 2021 (PNAS), which independently found dogs accompanied the first people into the Americas as human dispersal began ~15,000 years ago -- consistent with this ~14,600-year figure via a different dataset/method.
mrca.source_citation: Ní Leathlobhair et al. 2018, "The evolutionary history of dogs in the Americas," Science 361(6397):81-85

breeds.name: Basset Hound
breeds.estimate_note: "The Basset was reputedly bred by monks in France in the Middle Ages to hunt in heavy cover... though closely related to the entire family of French Bassets the breed was developed to perfection in Britain."
breeds.notes: "Middle Ages" is a broad era (~5th-15th century), not a precise date — flagged as anchor rather than rich since there's only the one imprecise era reference.

breeds.name: Great Pyrenees (Pyrenean Mountain Dog)
breeds.estimate_note: "Present in the Pyrenees from time immemorial... mentioned by Gaston Phoebus in the 14th century."
breeds.notes: Also dated: appreciated as companion dog in 17th century (court of Louis XIV); first detailed description 1897 (Count de Bylandt); first breed clubs ~1907; official FCI-lineage standard registered 1923.

breeds.name: English Mastiff
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Mastiff has been with us for many hundreds of years, and played its part in history since well before the Battle of Agincourt [1415], in the early fifteenth century.' Also: 'when the Romans invaded Britain they found a mastiff type dog already here, and were so impressed that they took some back to fight in the arenas of Rome.'
breeds.notes: The Roman 'mastiff type' claim refers to a type, not the named Mastiff breed. The pre-Agincourt reference (before 1415) is the earliest claim for the specific breed. Nearly extinct after WWII; revived through imports.

breeds.name: English Setter
breeds.estimate_note: AKC/ESAA (secondary; FCI-St N°2 has no historical section): 'breed originated in the 14th century, long before firearms existed.' First published reference: Dr. John Caius, De Canibus Britannicis (1570). Modern breed established by Edward Laverack from 1825.
breeds.notes: FCI standard (2009) has no historical summary section. AKC/ESAA cite 14th century origin; first written reference 1570. Modern breed shaped by Laverack (from 1825) and Llewellin. AKC recognition 1878 (one of 9 charter breeds).

breeds.name: Vizsla
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°57: "Written descriptions and graphic illustrations are found in documents of the 14th century already...modern breeding started in 1920...FCI recognition 1936."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source. Three dated refs: 14th century documentation, 1920 modern breeding, 1936 FCI recognition.

breeds.name: Shih Tzu
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: roots in Tibet, developed in China in imperial palaces. Wikipedia: 'favorites of the Chinese royals during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644)' with the Dowager Empress Cixi running a dedicated breeding program. First importation to Britain 1928 (Lady Brownrigg).
breeds.notes: Some sources claim earlier Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE) connection from Chinese art, but Ming Dynasty documentation is better-supported.

breeds.name: Borzoi (Russkaya Psovaya Borzaya)
breeds.estimate_note: "The history of the Borzoi dated from the XV century, to the Mongol invasion" — crossbred from Tatar sighthounds (Koutsi) and Russian Loshaya dogs, depicted in a prayer book belonging to Grand Prince Vasily III (early 1500s).
breeds.notes: Exceptionally dense timeline: Polish Greyhound blood added XVI-XVII centuries; large organized hunts with hundreds of dogs in XVIII-XIX centuries (the renowned Pershino hunt); first Congress of Borzoi lovers 1874; first standard adopted by Moscow Hunting Society 1888 (author N.P. Yermolov); standard revised repeatedly through 2006. One of the best multi-era histories found.

breeds.name: Beagle
breeds.estimate_note: "During the reigns of King Henry VIII and Queen Elizabeth I there were wirehaired Beagles, some of which were small enough to be carried in the pocket of a hunting jacket" — i.e. documented in England by the Tudor period (early-to-mid 1500s).
breeds.notes: Direct fci.be URL 404'd twice (tried g05 and a non-fci mirror that returned 403) before the correct g06-en suffix worked — worth remembering FCI version suffixes aren't guessable from other breeds' patterns, may need a couple of tries.

breeds.name: Havanese
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The breed comes from the Western Mediterranean region and has developed along the Spanish and Italian coastal region. It would seem that these dogs were imported early in Cuba by ocean navigating Italian captains.' Wikipedia: progenitors believed from Tenerife on Spanish colonial ships; Spanish colonization of Cuba began 1511.

breeds.name: Bichon Frise
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'brought to France from Italy during the Renaissance. In the 17th and 18th centuries, many renowned painters depicted these little dogs. The breed came back into fashion under Napoleon III. First registered in Belgium: Pitou, born 23 March 1924 (LOSH 1932). N°1 in French studbook (LOF): Ida, 18 October 1934. Current French name recognized 1978.'
breeds.notes: FCI says origin is France and Belgium. Renaissance introduction from Italy (15th-16th century). Popular in courts of 17th-18th centuries. Revived after WWI/WWII near-extinction. AKC recognition 1972.

breeds.name: Papillon
breeds.estimate_note: Secondary (FCI-St N°77 has no historical section): Continental Toy Spaniel (drop-eared Phalene variety) documented in court paintings from early 16th century. Erect-ear Papillon variety developed in 17th century court of Louis XIV; named for butterfly-like ear shape.
breeds.notes: FCI-St N°77 (1990/1998) has no historical summary section. Art evidence from early 16th century; erect-ear variety named Papillon developed 17th century. AKC recognition 1915.

breeds.name: Pug
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'as far back as the 1500s was being admired in the Netherlands... The Pug arrived in England when William III came to the throne [1689]. Until 1877 the breed was seen here only in fawn but in that year a black pair was introduced from the Orient.' Home country listed as China.
breeds.notes: Chinese origin (no date given for China). In Europe from 1500s via Dutch East India Company traders; in Netherlands and became symbol for Dutch royal patriots. In Britain from 1689 (William III). Black variety introduced 1877. AKC recognition 1885.

breeds.name: West Highland White Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "Scottish white terriers were recorded as early as during the reign of James VI of Scotland (1567-1625), who ordered a dozen of these white terriers from Argyll as a gift to France." Modern breed formalised in the 19th century.
breeds.notes: FCI N°85 (2010) has no historical section; Wikipedia gives earliest documentary reference under James VI.

breeds.name: Newfoundland
breeds.estimate_note: "The breed originated in the island of Newfoundland from indigenous dogs and the big black bear dog introduced by the Vikings after the year 1100... When the colonization of the island began in 1610, the Newfoundland Dog was already largely in possession of his proper morphology and natural behaviour."
breeds.notes: Two solid anchor dates (Viking introduction after 1100 AD; established type by 1610 colonization) — one of the better pre-1800s dated histories found.

breeds.name: Dalmatian
breeds.estimate_note: Dalmatians depicted on the altar painting "Madonna with Jesus and Angels" in Veli Losinj, Croatia, dating 1600-1630.
breeds.notes: FCI historical summary is unusually dense: church chronicles 1719 and 1737, Pennant's description 1771, Bewick 1790, first unofficial standard 1882, Dalmatian Club founded 1890, first FCI standard 1955.

breeds.name: Bulldog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Bulldog was first classified as such in the 1630s, though there is earlier mention of similar types referred to as bandogs.' After 1835 Cruelty to Animals Act the breed evolved for the show ring (first shown 1860).

breeds.name: Poodle (Standard)
breeds.estimate_note: FCI (N°172) covers all Poodle sizes as varieties of one breed. Wikipedia: 'Similar dogs date back to at least the 17th century'; German artist depictions of recognisably Poodle-type dogs from as early as the 17th century. FCI: 'In 1743, it was called the caniche' (naming reference, not origin date).
breeds.notes: Kaggle has separate keys for poodle-standard and poodle; FCI treats all sizes as one breed (FCI-St N°172). See also key 'poodle'. KC recognition 1874; AKC 1886. Origin disputed between Germany and France; no specific founding date established.

breeds.name: Saint Bernard
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'large mountain dogs have been kept since the middle of the 17th century for guarding and protection. The existence of such dogs has been documented pictorially since 1695 and in a written document at the hospice in the year 1707.'
breeds.notes: St. Bernard Pass hospice founded 11th century, but dogs documented there from mid-17th century (~1650). Pictorial: 1695. Written document at hospice: 1707. Genealogical records by Heinrich Schumacher: 1867. Swiss Dog Stud Book first entry 'Leon': Feb 1884. Swiss St. Bernard Club founded 15 March 1884. International recognition as Swiss breed: 2 June 1887.

breeds.name: Whippet
breeds.estimate_note: AKC (secondary; FCI-St N°162 has no historical section): breed developed in industrial Northern England (Lancashire/Yorkshire) by working class in late 18th-early 19th century, crossing small Greyhounds with terriers. KC recognition 1891, AKC 1888.
breeds.notes: FCI standard (2019) has no historical summary section. Breed development well-documented in secondary sources; consistently placed in late 18th-early 19th century Northern England. KC 1891; AKC 1888.

breeds.name: Pointer
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "Spanish Pointers were first introduced to England in 1713 by soldiers returning from Spain after the Peace of Utrecht." Breed refined as distinct English type through the 18th century.
breeds.notes: FCI N°1 (2009) has no historical section; Wikipedia used. AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Dachshund
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'The first verifiable references to the Dachshund... came from books written in the early 18th century.' FCI says 'has been known since the Middle Ages.' AKC claims 15th century but this predates verifiable written references. Oldest club (Deutsche Teckelklub) founded 1888.
breeds.notes: AKC/FCI claim Middle Ages or 15th century; earliest verifiable specific breed references are early 18th century. AKC claim not well-sourced.

breeds.name: Irish Setter
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'It was a clearly identifiable type in the 18th century. The Irish Red Setter Club was established in 1882 to promote the Breed. The club issued the Breed Standard in 1886.'
breeds.notes: FCI: derived from Irish Red and White Setter and an unknown solid red dog. Irish Red Setter Club established 1882; breed standard issued 1886.

breeds.name: Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°40: "Its existence for at least 200 years can be inferred from textual references to 'soft-coated' dogs." Standard dated 2001, so 200+ years = before 1801. Irish Kennel Club recognition 1937.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: English Foxhound
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°159: "bred along careful lines for over two hundred years, the stud books...dating back before 1800." FCI recognition 1964. Stud books pre-1800 are the earliest documentation.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Pomeranian
breeds.estimate_note: First recorded reference to the named Pomeranian: 2 November 1764, in James Boswell's diary. Queen Charlotte brought two Pomeranians to England in 1767. FCI: broader German Spitz family descends from 'stoneage Peat Dogs' — this applies to the Spitz type broadly, not the Pomeranian variety specifically.
breeds.notes: The 'stone age Peat Dogs' claim applies to the German Spitz type, not the Pomeranian as a distinct small variety. First breed club formed England 1891; AKC recognition 1900.

breeds.name: American Foxhound
breeds.estimate_note: Colonial English hounds in Virginia 17th-18th c; key event: 1785 Lafayette sent seven Grand Bleu de Gascogne to Washington who crossed them with Virginia pack; AKC 1886; FCI-St N°303 (1979/1998) has no historical section
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no history section; 1785 Lafayette–Washington gift documented at Mount Vernon; multiple independent secondary sources corroborate; AKC 1886

breeds.name: Labrador Retriever
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'Originally introduced to Great Britain in the late 1800s by Col Peter Hawker and the Earl of Malmesbury.' Breed club formed 1916.
breeds.notes: Kaggle lists origin as Canada; FCI standard attributes development to Great Britain from Newfoundland-type dogs.

breeds.name: Yakutian Laika
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°365: Multiple anchors — "archaeological discoveries confirm that the local people used dogs for sledding and hunting as far back as 8000 years ago. The very first references about dogs in this region date back to 1633. The first published account... Nicholas Witsen (Amsterdam, 1692). First description... 1843. First Breed Standard for the North-East Sled Dog was adopted in 1958." Year range here covers first historical reference (1633) to first formal standard (1958).
breeds.notes: Exceptionally well-documented origin with multiple dated references: archaeological evidence of local dog use 8000 BP, first historical reference 1633, first published account 1692 (Witsen, Amsterdam), first description "dog of a special breed" 1843, population census 1856 (15,157 sled dogs), first breed standard 1958. The 8000 BP archaeological claim is the Sakha/Yakut people using sled dogs generally — not necessarily the modern Yakutian Laika type specifically. The 1633 reference is the most defensible anchor for breed-level documentation.

breeds.name: Pharaoh Hound
breeds.estimate_note: CORRECTED FINDING — traditional claim vs. genetics disagree. Neither AKC nor FCI-St N°248 (1999, no historical section) states a date; popular sources repeat an "ancient Egypt" myth based on resemblance to tomb art of Anubis/jackal-headed gods. But genetic studies (Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, 2004, 85-breed DNA panel; a 2018 follow-up study) found the Pharaoh Hound only genetically diverged from the closely related Cirneco dell'Etna roughly 200 years ago — it is a comparatively MODERN reconstruction, not a surviving ancient lineage. The "Egyptian myth" is explicitly contradicted by DNA evidence.
breeds.notes: IMPORTANT: this is the opposite problem from most other vague-tier breeds — not "missing data," but "the popular/traditional claim is actively wrong." On the timeline, this breed likely belongs near the 1800s (recent breed formation), NOT the ancient end, despite AKC calling it "ancient." Flag prominently — this contradicts the general vibe of the project's ancient-breed narrative and is exactly the kind of claim worth fact-checking before publishing.

breeds.name: Australian Shepherd
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°342 (2009): 'developed exclusively in the United States. The Australian Shepherd was given its name because of the association with Basque Sheepherders who came to the United States from Australia in the 1800s.' SECONDARY: Basque shepherd dogs (likely Pyrenean Sheepdogs) arrived from Australia in late 1800s; formalized in American West. ASCA (Australian Shepherd Club of America) founded 1957. AKC recognition 1993.
breeds.notes: Developed in American West in the 1800s from Basque sheepherder dogs arriving from Australia. 'Only in America' story: European-origin dogs developed exclusively in USA. ASCA founded 1957; AKC recognized 1993. FCI-St N°342 (2009). Worklist primary is AKC page; used FCI standard as better source. Genetic origin is European (likely Pyrenean Sheepdogs), formal breed development and naming in USA.

breeds.name: Scottish Deerhound
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "the modern breed...only became widely known as the Scottish Deerhound related to English regional greyhounds...in the early 19th century." The Cadboll Stone (~1200 years ago) shows deer hunt with large dogs, but Wikipedia notes genetics have not connected that carving to the modern breed.
breeds.notes: Previously vague; Wikipedia distinguishes modern breed (early 19th century) from ancient art depictions whose genetic link to the breed is unverified.

breeds.name: Weimaraner
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°99: "the Weimaraner...was already kept at the Weimar court in the first third of the 19th century [1800-1833]...from about 1890 on, the breed was produced according to a plan...pure bred since 1900."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Gordon Setter
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: Alexander, 4th Duke of Gordon (1743-1827) established his Black and Tan Setter kennel at Gordon Castle, Fochabers, Scotland (after 1786); breed brought to USA by Daniel Webster in 1842; AKC recognition 1892; KC formally named "Gordon Setter" 1924.
breeds.notes: FCI N°6 (2016) has no historical section; Wikipedia used. The 4th Duke's kennel (early 19th century) is the founding event.

breeds.name: Parson Russell Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "In 1819 [Rev. John Russell] purchased a small white and tan terrier bitch named Trump from a milkman...She formed the basis for his breeding programme." By the 1850s recognised as a distinct Fox Terrier type.
breeds.notes: FCI N°339 has no historical date; Wikipedia used as secondary source.

breeds.name: American Bulldog
breeds.estimate_note: Working English Bulldogs brought to American South after UK bull-baiting ban (1835); near extinction post-WWII; revived by John D. Johnson and Alan Scott; UKC recognized January 1, 1999
breeds.notes: UKC primary source has historical section; 1835 date is the UK Cruelty to Animals Act banning bull-baiting

breeds.name: Australian Cattle Dog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°287 (2012): 'developed to assist with establishing the cattle industry in early Australian conditions' via crossing blue merle Collies with Dingo, later Dalmatian and Kelpie. No years in standard. SECONDARY: Thomas Simpson Hall (1808-1870) crossed Scottish Highland Collies with Dingoes in the 1840s creating Hall's Heelers at Dartbrook station, Hunter Valley NSW. Bagust brothers refined with Dalmatian and Black and Tan Kelpie late 19th c. Robert Kaleski produced first breed standard in 1903.
breeds.notes: FCI-St N°287 (2012) gives development story but no specific years. Secondary sources (acdca.org, Australian Cattle Dog Society of GB): Hall's Heelers ~1840s; first breed standard 1903 (Kaleski). AKC recognition 1980. Worklist primary is AKC but FCI standard has more history. Origin is mid-19th century selective development from Dingo x Scottish Highland Collie crosses.

breeds.name: Leonberger
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°145: "At end of thirties, beginning of forties of 19th century, Heinrich Essig...crossed a Newfoundland bitch with a 'Barry' male from monastery hospice Grand St.Bernhard...The first dogs really called 'Leonbergers' were born in 1846."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Kerry Blue Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°3: "The first probable literary references to the Kerry Blue date from 1847, the author describes a bluish slate coloured dog...prevalent in Kerry." First show appearance 1913; Dublin Blue Terrier Club formed 1920.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Rough Collie
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Rough Collie is the somewhat refined version of the original working collie of the Scottish shepherd, from which it has been selected over at least a hundred years.' FCI also notes breed evolved from dogs brought to Scotland by Romans mating with native types.
breeds.notes: FCI gives no specific date; Roman-era dogs crossed with native types as ancestors. Modern show breed developed through 19th-century selection. Queen Victoria popularized breed from 1860s; AKC recognition 1885. Same breed stock as Smooth Collie (FCI-St N°296).

breeds.name: Smooth Collie
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°156 (Rough Collie): 'The rough and the smooth Collie is the same with the exception of coat length... evolved from dogs brought to Scotland by the Romans... selected over at least a hundred years.'
breeds.notes: FCI-St N°296 (2021) has no historical summary section. Identical origin to Rough Collie; same stock, differing only in coat type. AKC recognition 1885 (as Collie varieties).

breeds.name: Miniature Pinscher
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°185: "kept in large numbers around the turn of the century already; Stud Book for 1925 records no less than 1300 entries." Established breed by late 19th century.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Jack Russell Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°345: "originated in England in the 1800's due to the efforts of the Reverend John Russell; he developed a strain of Fox Terriers."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; UKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Wire Fox Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "developed in England by fox hunting enthusiasts; believed to be descended from a now-extinct rough-coated, black-and-tan working terrier of Wales, Derbyshire, and Durham." Fox Terrier Club founded 1875.
breeds.notes: FCI N°169 (2009) has no historical section; Wikipedia used.

breeds.name: Bullmastiff
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°157: "evolved from the Old English Mastiff and the Bulldog; primarily used as guard dog to help the gamekeeper in the apprehension of poachers." KC recognized 1924, AKC 1933.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section brief; Wikipedia confirms 19th century gamekeeper use. AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Chesapeake Bay Retriever
breeds.estimate_note: AKC Judges guide: "by the late 1800s, a distinctive dog known as the Chesapeake Bay Duck dog was recognized as a breed." Roots traced to two Newfoundlands (Sailor and Canton); light colors in Maryland as early as the 1840s.
breeds.notes: AKC Judges guide PDF used as primary source.

breeds.name: Yorkshire Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Yorkshire Terrier was first seen around the 1850s.' Developed from old Black and Tan Terrier crossed with Maltese and Skye Terrier by Scottish mill workers who migrated to Yorkshire. Current name accepted 1870.

breeds.name: Flat-Coated Retriever
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "Originating in the mid-19th century in England...first examples introduced around 1860, final type established ~1880. From 1873 a 'stable type' per AKC." Ancestry includes Newfoundland, Collie-type, Setter blood. AKC recognition 1915.
breeds.notes: FCI N°121 (2009) and Kaggle primary source (Sporting Group PDF) lack breed-specific history; Wikipedia used.

breeds.name: Airedale Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: "In the mid-19th century, working-class people created the Airedale Terrier by crossing the old English rough-coated Black and Tan Terrier with the Otterhound." First exhibited at a championship dog show in 1864; named "Airedale Terrier" 1879; KC recognition 1886.
breeds.notes: Previously vague; Wikipedia provides first-show date 1864 and naming/recognition dates.

breeds.name: Staffordshire Bull Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 2017 genome-wide study placed all bull and terrier-type dogs' origins at 1860-1870, corresponding to historical descriptions of dog fighting in Ireland and undocumented crosses at that period. 'In 1930, the name Staffordshire Bull Terrier first appeared in advertisements.' KC recognition 1935.
breeds.notes: FCI standard (1987) has no historical summary section. Bull and terrier crosses developed after Cruelty to Animals Act 1835 shifted breeders from bull-baiting to dog fighting. FCI recognition 1954; AKC 1974.

breeds.name: Golden Retriever
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: In 1868, Dudley Marjoribanks (later Lord Tweedmouth) mated Nous (yellow Flat-coated Retriever, b.1864) to Belle (Tweed Water Spaniel), producing the first four yellow pups documented in his stud book (1868-1890), held at the Kennel Club library.
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no historical summary section. KC recognition 1913 (as Retriever Golden or Yellow); name changed to Golden Retriever 1920.

breeds.name: Boston Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'The Boston terrier breed originated around 1870, when Robert C. Hooper of Boston purchased... a dog named Judge (known later as Hooper's Judge).' Judge mated to Gyp formed the breed foundation. Boston Terrier Club formed 1891; AKC admitted 1893.
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no historical summary section.

breeds.name: Dobermann
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: Friedrich Louis Dobermann (1834-1894), a tax collector and part-time dog catcher, bred dogs in the 1870s crossing 'butcher's dogs' (early Rottweiler type) with Thuringian shepherd dogs to produce alert protective housedogs.

breeds.name: Australian Kelpie
breeds.estimate_note: ANKC Extended Breed Standard (FCI PRE N°293): "In the early 1870's Mr. Robertson of Yeraldra Station (near Forbes in NSW) imported a dog and bitch, Brutus and Jennie from Scotland." "King's Kelpie was entered in the first Sheepdog Trial in 1872, which was held in Forbes, New South Wales. She won this Trial with ease. After this trail win her pups were in great demand and at the time were called Kelpie's pups, and so the name evolved." Breed originated from Scottish Rutherford/North Country collies crossed in Australia in the early 1870s.
breeds.notes: The AKC FSS PDF (listed as primary source in dog_breed_sources.csv) has an empty History section — no content. FCI PRE standard (N°293, ANKC Extended Breed Standard, 1994) contains the full documented history and was used instead. The breed is a modern creation (1870s Australia) from imported Scottish working collies. "Kelpie" is a Gaelic word meaning "water sprite," taken from the name of the founding bitch, Gleeson's Kelpie.

breeds.name: English Springer Spaniel
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: descended from Norfolk/Shropshire Spaniels, shown as 'Norfolk Spaniel' by the 1850s. John Caius described the spaniel type in 1576 (not breed-specific). In 1899, first joint trials held; KC recognized English Springer Spaniel as a distinct breed in 1902. FCI: 'oldest of sporting gundogs' (no specific date).
breeds.notes: FCI historical summary is vague ('ancient and pure origins'). Wikipedia traces the specific breed type to Norfolk/Shropshire Spaniels of the 1850s; formally recognized by KC 1902, AKC 1910.

breeds.name: Great Dane (Deutsche Dogge)
breeds.estimate_note: Forerunners were the "Bullenbeisser" and "Hatz- and Saurüden" (hunting/wild boar hounds), a mix between Mastiff and Greyhound types, generically called "Dogge." In 1878 a committee of seven breeders/judges in Berlin (chaired by Dr. Bodinus) decided to classify all these varieties as one breed, "Deutsche Doggen." First standard laid down in 1880 at a Berlin show.
breeds.notes: No ancient-era claim for this one (breed formation is explicitly a 19th-century administrative act, not a claimed ancient lineage) — good clean case with no debunking-caveat needed.

breeds.name: English Cocker Spaniel
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'Cocker Spaniels were recognized as a separate breed from Field and Springer Spaniels soon after the formation of the Kennel Club in 1873. He originated as the cocking spaniel, and derived this name from flushing woodcock.'
breeds.notes: Type (cocking spaniel) predates Kennel Club formation. Formal breed recognition as distinct from Field/Springer Spaniels in the 1870s-1880s (Spaniel Club founded 1885).

breeds.name: Scottish Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°73: "Scottish Terrier Club formed 1882, just three years after the start of the breed as we know it today by Capt Gordon Murray"; first standard drawn up 1881.
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Samoyed
breeds.estimate_note: British zoologist Ernest Kilburn Scott spent three months among Samoyed tribes in 1889 and brought dogs back to England ("Sabarka," "Whitey Petchora," "Musti"), forming the base of the Western Samoyed.
breeds.notes: First standard written in England in 1909. No date for the breed's actual origin among Samoyed tribes, only for its introduction to the West.

breeds.name: French Bulldog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: first breed club founded in Paris 1880; first dog shown at exhibition 1887; first standard and French KC recognition 1898.

breeds.name: Miniature Schnauzer
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: Rough-haired Pinscher first shown at Hanover 1879; recorded in German Hundestammbuch 1880; first breed society Pinscherklub formed 1895. FCI standard: breed emerged 'around the turn of the century' (~1900). FCI accepted Miniature Schnauzer as separate entry 1955.

breeds.name: Border Collie
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'Old Hemp (born September 1893, Northumberland, England) is the foundation sire of the Border Collie; all purebred Border Collies can trace their ancestry back to him.' The name 'border collie' coined 1915 by ISDS Secretary James Reid.
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no historical summary section. Broader landrace collie type predates 1893; the modern breed is defined by Old Hemp (b. 1893).

breeds.name: Boxer
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'In 1895, Friedrich Robert, Elard König, and R. Höpner... founded the first Boxer Club, the Deutschen Boxer Club.' First Boxer show held Munich 1896. FCI: 'The small, so called Brabant Bullenbeisser is regarded as the immediate ancestor of the Boxer.'
breeds.notes: AKC registered first Boxer 1904; recognition year here is AKC's first registration.

breeds.name: German Shorthaired Pointer
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Zuchtbuch Deutsch-Kurzhaar (Studbook) has been published since 1897.' Breed developed from pointing dogs (Spanish, French, Flemish) into a versatile gundog after mid-18th century.

breeds.name: American Pit Bull Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: 19th-c England/Ireland/Scotland Bulldog × Terrier crosses for dog fighting; brought to America; UKC founded 1898 specifically for APBT; C.Z. Bennett assigned registration #1 to his dog Bennetts Ring in 1898
breeds.notes: UKC primary source has historical section; 1898 UKC founding around the APBT is the formal recognition anchor

breeds.name: German Shepherd Dog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The Verein für Deutsche Schäferhunde (SV) was established at Frankfurt/Main on 20 September 1899 according to suggestions by A. Meyer and Max von Stephanitz; methodical breeding of the German Shepherd Dog was started in 1899.'

breeds.name: Belgian Malinois
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The breed was officially born between 1891 and 1897. On September 29th, 1891, the Belgian Shepherd Dog Club was founded in Brussels... by April 3rd, 1892, a first detailed breed standard had already been drawn up... it wasn't until 1901 that the first Belgian Shepherds were registered with the Royal Saint-Hubert Society Stud Book... by 1910 the type and temperament of the Belgian Shepherd had been established.'
breeds.notes: All four Belgian Shepherd varieties (Groenendael/Sheepdog, Tervueren, Malinois, Laekenois) covered by FCI-St N°15. Belgian Shepherd Dog Club founded 1891; first standard 1892; first stud book registrations 1901; type established 1910. Named for Malines (Mechelen), Belgium.

breeds.name: Belgian Tervuren
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The breed was officially born between 1891 and 1897. On September 29th, 1891, the Belgian Shepherd Dog Club was founded in Brussels... by April 3rd, 1892, a first detailed breed standard had already been drawn up... it wasn't until 1901 that the first Belgian Shepherds were registered with the Royal Saint-Hubert Society Stud Book... by 1910 the type and temperament of the Belgian Shepherd had been established.'
breeds.notes: All four Belgian Shepherd varieties covered by FCI-St N°15. Same origin dates as Belgian Malinois. Named for village of Tervuren, Belgium.

breeds.name: Belgian Sheepdog
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'The breed was officially born between 1891 and 1897. On September 29th, 1891, the Belgian Shepherd Dog Club was founded in Brussels... by April 3rd, 1892, a first detailed breed standard had already been drawn up... it wasn't until 1901 that the first Belgian Shepherds were registered with the Royal Saint-Hubert Society Stud Book... by 1910 the type and temperament of the Belgian Shepherd had been established.'
breeds.notes: All four Belgian Shepherd varieties covered by FCI-St N°15. The Belgian Sheepdog = Groenendael variety. Same origin dates as Belgian Malinois. Named for Chateau de Groenendael near Brussels.

breeds.name: Bernese Mountain Dog
breeds.estimate_value_raw: 1902-1910 (breed formalization); ancestral farm dog origin pre-1900s
breeds.estimate_note: Farm dog of ancestral origin in prealpine regions around Bern; originally named 'Dürrbächler' after hamlet near Riggisberg. Exhibited at shows 1902, 1904, 1907; breed club 'Schweizerischer Dürrbach-Klub' founded 1907; 107 specimens shown at Burgdorf in 1910.
breeds.notes: Multiple dated milestones: 1902-1910 formalization with specific show dates and club founding.

breeds.name: Afghan Hound
breeds.estimate_note: "The first Afghans arrived in Britain in the early 1900s and one, called Zardin, won in spectacular style at the 1907 Crystal Palace show in London."
breeds.notes: Only dates are about the breed's arrival/show history in Britain, nothing about origin in Afghanistan itself — needs a secondary source for the actual origin era.

breeds.name: Brittany
breeds.estimate_note: FCI: 'Probably one of the oldest of the spaniel type dogs, improved at the beginning of the 20th century by diverse outcrosses and selections. A draft of a breed standard drawn up in Nantes in 1907 was presented and adopted at the first General Assembly held in Loudéac, June 7, 1908. This was the first standard of the Naturally Short-Tailed Brittany Spaniel Club.'
breeds.notes: FCI notes it is 'probably one of the oldest of the spaniel type dogs' but gives no specific ancient date. Recording 1908 as the formal breed standardization date.

breeds.name: Shetland Sheepdog
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'The year 1909 marked the initial recognition of the Shetland by the English Kennel Club, with the first registered Shetland being a female called Badenock Rose.' AKC recognition 1911 (first registered: Lord Scott).
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no historical summary section.

breeds.name: Rottweiler
breeds.estimate_note: "Considered to be one of the oldest dog breeds. Its origin goes back to Roman times... marched over the Alps with the Roman legions... In the region of Rottweil, these dogs met and mixed with the native dogs." Named for Rottweil, known as the "Rottweil butcher's dog." Tested for police service in the early 20th century and officially recognized as police dogs in 1910.
breeds.notes: First pull using the new pdftotext pipeline (see PROCESS.md) — curl + pdftotext -layout instead of WebFetch/Read, ~40x smaller file to process. No exact date for the Roman-era claim itself ("Roman times" is qualitative), but 1910 police-dog recognition is a hard date.

breeds.name: Rhodesian Ridgeback
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°146: "The original standard, which was drafted by F.R.Barnes, in Bulawayo, Rhodesia, in 1922, was based on that of the Dalmatian and was approved by the South African Kennel Union in 1926."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: East Siberian Laika
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°305: "The first description of the pre-Amur Laika, which later become the basis of the breed standard, dates from the beginning of the 20th century. In 1947 East-Siberian Laika achieved breed status." Evolved from Tungus, Yakut, pre-Baikal and pre-Amur Laikas.
breeds.notes: Breed status achieved 1947; provisional standard 1949; final standard 1981. The breed evolved from regional Siberian Laika types; not a landrace but a 20th-century consolidation of existing regional types.

breeds.name: Shiba Inu
breeds.estimate_note: Dense multi-date history: native to Japan "since the primitive ages"; English Setters/Pointers imported 1868-1912 causing crossbreeding; pure Shiba became scarce by 1912-1926; preservation effort began ~1928; breed standard unified 1934; designated a "natural monument" in 1937.
breeds.notes: One of the richest/most precisely dated modern-era histories found — good model for how a breed can lack an ancient date but still have a full dated story.

breeds.name: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: In 1926, Roswell Eldridge offered Crufts prizes to recreate the old flat-faced Blenheim Spaniel type; first Cavalier club formed 1928; KC recognition as distinct breed 5 December 1944.
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no historical summary section. The Cavalier is a modern recreation of the 17th-century flat-faced spaniel type depicted in Van Dyck paintings, deliberately bred in the 1920s-40s.

breeds.name: American Staffordshire Terrier
breeds.estimate_note: Same 19th-c bull-and-terrier origin as APBT; AKC recognized 1936 as 'Staffordshire Terrier'; renamed 'American Staffordshire Terrier' 1972; FCI-St N°286 (1997) has no historical section
breeds.notes: FCI standard has no history section; AKC 1936 recognition and 1972 rename from secondary sources

breeds.name: American Cocker Spaniel
breeds.estimate_note: FCI-St N°167 (2021) has no historical section; AKC page blocked; American type diverged from English Cocker Spaniel during early 20th c; AKC recognized separately 1946; broader spaniel history traces to 14th c
breeds.notes: Primary source (FCI 2021) has no historical section; AKC page blocked; 1946 AKC separate breed recognition from secondary sources

breeds.name: Dogo Argentino
breeds.estimate_note: FCI N°292: "creator was Dr. Antonio Nores Martinez (1907-1956)...In 1947 the breed was already created and its genotype and phenotype were stabilized. The same year the breed standard was presented at the Hunter's Club in the City of Buenos Aires."
breeds.notes: FCI historical section used; AKC is Kaggle primary source.

breeds.name: Cane Corso
breeds.estimate_note: Wikipedia: 'The modern breed derives from selective breeding from about 1980 of a few surviving animals' following near-extinction after Italian sharecropping collapsed in the 1960s. FCI: 'Its direct ancestor is the old Roman Molossian' (no date given for ancient ancestor).
breeds.notes: Recording 1980 as the modern standardized breed revival date. Ancient Roman Molossian ancestor claim noted; no specific date given in FCI standard. Società Amatori Cane Corso formed 1983; ENCI recognition 1994; FCI provisional 1996; FCI full 2007; AKC 2010.

breeds.name: Silken Windhound
breeds.estimate_note: UKC breed standard + ISWS (https://silkenwindhounds.org/history-of-the-breed/): "Silken Windhounds arrived as a breed with the 'D' litter whelped in 1985." Founded by Francie Stull (Kristull Kennel) using Borzoi, Whippet-based lurchers, and Whippets. Breed name officially adopted 1998; ISWS chartered 1999; UKC recognition March 18, 2011.
breeds.notes: Very recent breed with fully documented history. Founded by Francie Stull at Kristull Kennel. Key dates: first litter 1985, name adopted 1998, ISWS chartered 1999, UKC recognition 2011. Foundation crosses were Borzoi (structural base and coat) + small Whippet-based lurchers + Whippets (size and coursing). The breed fills a gap between small and large sighthounds (18-24 inches at shoulder, silky coat).

breeds.name: Tamaskan Dog
breeds.estimate_note: Tamaskan Dog Register (TDR) official history: "the first generation of registered Tamaskan Dogs was born in May 2006 at Alba in Scotland. At the same time, the Tamaskan Dog Registry (TDR) was founded for the purpose of overseeing the development of the breed." Foundation stock traces to 1980s Arctic-breed mixes imported to England, the 1998-founded Northern Inuit breed, a 2002 split forming the Utonagan, and a 2004 outcross to Reijo Jaaskelainen's Polar Speed Kennels (Lapland, Finland) racing huskies. Named from "Tamaska" ("mighty wolf" in Munsee/Delawarian).
breeds.notes: A rare case among 'ancient'-framed breeds in this dataset: Tamaskan Dog is a deliberately, recently created breed with a genuinely well-documented paper trail (unlike most rows here, no ancient-claim verification is needed -- there is no ancient claim). Not recognized by AKC or FCI; recognized by ARBA and KCUSA (Oct 2013), later ICE/IABCA/ICKC (2017). Four named breed founders (Lynn Sharkey/Hardey, Jennie Peacock/Saxby, Liz Wilson, Zee Turner). TDR itself notes the breed is 'not officially recognized in Finland' despite being primarily developed there. Added 2026-08-09 per user request; not in the original Kaggle dog_breed_sources.csv worklist (marked review_status=seeded there), so also added to that file directly.

undated.name: Anatolian Shepherd Dog (Çoban Köpeği)
undated.notes: fci.be direct PDF for FCI-St N°331 gave a 404 on the URL pattern tried; this mirror (a US breed club site) had the same standard text and was readable directly by WebFetch (no PDF binary issue) — a useful fallback source type.

undated.name: Greyhound
undated.notes: FCI acknowledges experts are 'not unanimous' about the Egyptian/Middle Eastern origin claim (4000 BC). Parker et al. 2017 genomics study (Cell Reports, 161 breeds) found Greyhound has roots in Celtic herding dogs — analogous to the art-resemblance myths debunked for Pharaoh Hound/Ibizan Hound. Modern standard breed developed in Britain. Cannot confirm 4000 BC date against genetics.

undated.name: Cairn Terrier
undated.notes: FCI N°4 (1987) has no historical section; Wikipedia confirms old but undated origin.

village_dogs.name: Taiwan / Indonesian village dog basal clade
village_dogs.diverged_from: broader southern East Asian dog lineage
village_dogs.estimate_note: Zhang et al. 2020 whole-genome analysis integrated a real Taiwan village dog sample with 97 published canid genomes; found it groups within a basal southern-East-Asia/Island-Southeast-Asia clade (the same clade that produced dingoes and New Guinea Singing Dogs), with clade divergence from Indonesian village dogs dated to ~9,900 years ago. Consistent with the broader <16,300-year regional dog-origin estimate south of the Yangtze River (Pang et al. 2009).
village_dogs.notes: Pilot row for this schema (see village_dog_populations_schema.md). This date currently also lives in breed_origins.csv's taiwan-dog row (origin_estimate_value: ~9900 years ago) as a proxy for that breed's landrace date -- the same tier-conflation ancestor_lineages.csv was built to resolve, one tier over. Migrating taiwan-dog to reference this row via village_dog_population_id (with its own origin_estimate_type reset to none) is the natural first real usage of this file. Only clean village-dog pilot case as of 2026-08-09 -- Dingo/NGSD are feral/wild, a different category (see schema doc); Central Asian and African village dog populations are genetically established but have no dated divergence estimate in the literature found so far.
village_dogs.source_citation: Zhang et al. 2020, "Genomic regions under selection in the feralization of the dingoes," Nature Communications

village_dogs.name: Middle Eastern village dog clade
village_dogs.region: Middle East (Egypt, Lebanon, Qatar, Turkey, Afghanistan sampled)
village_dogs.diverged_from: reciprocally monophyletic sister clade to the Southeast Asian village dog Y-chromosome lineage
village_dogs.estimate_note: Brown et al. 2011 Y-chromosome (paternal lineage) analysis found Middle Eastern village dogs form a reciprocally monophyletic clade distinct from the Southeast Asian village dog clade, estimated age 6,820 BP (95% CI 3,931-9,709 BP). Desert-bred Salukis clustered entirely within this clade, sharing six haplotypes with regional village dogs.
village_dogs.notes: Second real dated village-dog population found (2026-08-09), after the Taiwan/Indonesian pilot -- schema was deliberately not generalized further until a second real case showed up (see village_dog_populations_schema.md). Y-chromosome-only (paternal lineage), wide confidence interval (3,931-9,709 BP) -- weaker/narrower evidence than Zhang et al. 2020's whole-genome dating for the Taiwan/Indonesian clade, hence anchor not rich. Does not establish when the modern standardized Saluki breed itself was founded, only that it clusters within this dated regional clade -- Saluki's own tier-2 date (FCI/AKC's ~3300 BCE Sumerian-pendant claim) is separate, unaffected, and itself flagged in that row's notes as an unverified resemblance-based claim (same epistemic category as the debunked Pharaoh Hound/Ibizan Hound tomb-art dates) -- this clade date doesn't confirm or contradict that specific number, just establishes a deeper, genetically-real clade Saluki belongs to.
village_dogs.source_citation: Brown et al. 2011, "Phylogenetic distinctiveness of Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian village dog Y chromosomes illuminates dog origins," PLoS ONE 6(12):e28496

village_dogs_undated.name: Central Asian village dog
village_dogs_undated.notes: Embark's Central Asian Village Dog page (embarkvet.com) claims "over 15,000 years" of ancestry with no citation whatsoever -- checked twice (2026-08-09), no footnotes/references/external links to any scientific source anywhere on the page. The real underlying research, Shannon et al. 2015 (PNAS, "Genetic structure in village dogs reveals a Central Asian domestication origin"), found Central Asia has the lowest linkage-disequilibrium decay among sampled village dog populations (their proxy for closest-to-ancestral), but explicitly states SNP array data cannot estimate the timing of ancient population events -- gives no date. The origin claim itself is also disputed (Wang et al. 2016 PNAS directly challenged it). No divergence-time estimate found anywhere for this population as of 2026-08-09 -- recorded as none/vague rather than using Embark's unsourced figure. Revisit if a real dated ancient-DNA study surfaces; see tasks.md and village_dog_populations_schema.md for the full history.
